primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reported fiscal Q1 Mar 12 and withdrew annual guidance citing lacking visibility and intensifying demand uncertainty. Expected ~$5.7B current-quarter revenue below prior Street
secondary_factors: Broad chip and supply-chain fear from COVID plus March 16 market panic
store_description: Broadcom's March 12 update was not just macro noise — management explicitly withdrew annual guidance and flagged worsening visibility despite saying Q1 itself had not yet seen a material COVID impact. Into March 16 that made AVGO especially vulnerable.

primary_cause: No major Amazon-specific negative. Mar 16 announced hiring 100,000 warehouse and delivery workers and $2/hr raise — demand-positive but mixed for margins
secondary_factors: Rising fulfillment and labor costs. Fear of operational strain in warehouses. March 16 de-risking wave. Broad market panic
store_description: The main fresh Amazon-specific news was supportive for revenue but mixed for margins. The 5.4% decline was probably not about collapsing demand but a combination of market-wide liquidation plus investor concern that COVID would pressure logistics costs and execution.

primary_cause: No material American Tower-specific negative Mar 13-15. Sector-wide REIT and liquidity and rate panic
secondary_factors: Forced deleveraging. Fear around capital markets access. Indiscriminate selling of defensive equities during crash
store_description: AMT's 15.2% fall was too large to ignore but no meaningful company-specific catalyst in the prior 3 days. This looks like a March 16 cross-asset liquidation in which even high-quality infrastructure REITs were sold aggressively as investors rushed for cash.

primary_cause: No major Amgen-specific negative. Amgen Foundation committing up to $12.5M in relief. Mar 10 highlighted five-year Aimovig data. Mostly broad market drawdown
secondary_factors: Biotech risk-off selling. General fear around healthcare utilization disruption. Available news flow was neutral or mildly positive
store_description: No strong stock-specific bearish trigger for Amgen in the 3 days before the drop. The 6.6% decline looks more like biotech being pulled down with the March 16 liquidation than a reaction to company fundamentals.

primary_cause: Sector-wide semiconductor repricing on COVID disruption risk. No major AMD-specific negative Mar 13-15
secondary_factors: General market panic. Sympathy with Broadcom Intel Applied-style semiconductor exposure. Broader semiconductor complex under pressure
store_description: AMD's drop looks primarily like a semis basket selloff rather than a response to an AMD-specific corporate event. With manufacturers reporting broad disruption concerns and investors reassessing both supply and end demand AMD got hit along with the rest of the chip group.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Reported Q1 Mar 12 — record revenue $3.09B but Q2 target ~$3.175B. Management said customers in harder-hit countries reducing spending. $0.07/share hit from canceled events
secondary_factors: Multiple compression in high-growth software during March 16 crash. Virus-related caution plus broad Nasdaq liquidation
store_description: Adobe's setup was more fragile than a casual look suggests: Q1 was strong but management already signaled softer customer spending in affected geographies and guided Q2 revenue to roughly $3.175B. In a market suddenly unwilling to pay premium multiples that combination drove the 14.7% decline.

primary_cause: Fear COVID would hurt consulting and discretionary enterprise spending. Accenture reported fiscal Q2 Mar 19 — updated FY2020 outlook to reflect expected coronavirus impact
secondary_factors: Broad market de-risking in services and IT names. Revenue $11.14B EPS $1.91 bookings $14.2B. Solid numbers but investors looking through toward sudden freeze in client projects
store_description: Accenture's actual quarterly numbers were solid but investors were looking through them toward a sudden freeze in client projects and discretionary tech spending. The company's own language about updating outlook for coronavirus impact reinforced that.

primary_cause: No negative Abbott-specific catalyst. Major COVID testing product announcements came later. Mostly broad-market and medtech and utilization fear
secondary_factors: Concern elective procedures and routine diagnostics would be disrupted by pandemic
store_description: Abbott was not yet getting the later boost from its rapid COVID tests and there does not appear to have been a stock-specific negative headline in the prior 3 days. Investors selling diversified medtech and diagnostics names on the view that hospital systems and routine care volumes would be disrupted.

primary_cause: No major AbbVie-specific negative Mar 13-15. Allergan deal old news. Risk-off selling in large-cap pharma with deal and leverage overhang
secondary_factors: Market stress. Concern Allergan acquisition increased balance-sheet sensitivity in suddenly risk-averse tape
store_description: AbbVie's 13% decline appears larger than what pure defensiveness would imply. The most plausible reason is that investors treated it as less safe pharma because of the still-pending Allergan transaction and associated leverage. No new bearish headline in the prior 3 days.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Apple announced Mar 14 would close all retail stores outside Greater China until Mar 27. Already warned Feb about missing guidance due to COVID supply and demand damage
secondary_factors: Existing iPhone supply-chain concerns from China. Broader tech selloff. Direct expression of both supply-chain risk and collapsing physical retail activity
store_description: Apple had already warned in February that it would miss guidance and then on March 14 took the highly visible step of closing all stores outside Greater China through March 27. That made AAPL a direct expression of both supply-chain risk and collapsing physical retail activity.

primary_cause: Actually POSITIVE news — Mar 13 announced Janssen collaboration with Beth Israel to accelerate COVID-19 vaccine candidate. Broad market selloff not company-specific negative
secondary_factors: Broad healthcare selloff. Uncertainty over non-COVID business volumes. Positive vaccine headline could not offset March 16 panic
store_description: JNJ actually had constructive virus-related news right before the drop announcing a vaccine collaboration and manufacturing scale-up preparations. Because that headline was positive the 5.3% decline looks mostly attributable to the March 16 market panic.

primary_cause: No clear Colgate-specific negative Mar 13-15. Indiscriminate consumer staples selling during liquidity panic
secondary_factors: Emerging concerns around global supply chains and FX and exposure to international markets
store_description: Colgate's drop was unusually steep for a staples name and no company-specific news trigger was found. CL was caught in the March 16 liquidation wave with investors temporarily selling even defensive global consumer names as they raised cash.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Comcast announced COVID-response steps Mar 16 including making current movies available at home. Later said COVID would materially impact results delay film distribution and close theme parks
secondary_factors: Advertising risk. General market selloff. NBCUniversal theme-park film and advertising exposure highly vulnerable to shutdowns
store_description: Comcast was not just a cable and internet story. Investors were also repricing its exposure to movie distribution advertising and theme parks as lockdowns accelerated. The company's own later statement that COVID would materially impact operations strongly supports that March 16 selling was tied to real shutdown risk.

primary_cause: Semiconductor equipment supply-chain shock expectations. No Mar 13-15 company release. Later Mar 23 withdrew Q2 guidance
secondary_factors: High beta to cyclical capex plus market crash. Applied's business depended on global manufacturing and logistics chain that COVID was disrupting in real time
store_description: The exact guidance withdrawal came one week later but the underlying problem was already visible: Applied's business depended on a global manufacturing and logistics chain that COVID was disrupting in real time. Investors seem to have priced that in aggressively on March 16.

primary_cause: Not about weak demand — Costco reported Feb adjusted comp sales rose 11.7% from virus-driven buying. Broad-market selling plus concern about operating strain and costs
secondary_factors: Margin pressure from labor sanitation crowd control and panic-buying distortions. Relatively smaller drop versus market
store_description: Costco's pre-drop news flow was actually strong on sales with virus-driven pantry loading lifting comps. That makes the 6.3% decline look less like a demand story and more like a risk-off move in which investors worried that extraordinary traffic staffing and sanitation costs would temporarily compress margins.

primary_cause: Fear of sudden small-business recession hitting QuickBooks and payments exposure. Highly exposed to small-business health. Later filings said mid-March COVID began negatively affecting small-business results
secondary_factors: High-multiple software derating. Uncertainty around tax-season timing. No fresh Mar 13-15 earnings release
store_description: Intuit's decline makes sense as a forward-looking repricing of SMB stress rather than a reaction to one headline. The company later acknowledged that mid-March COVID was hurting small-business results and investors on March 16 were already anticipating shutdown damage.

primary_cause: Oil price collapse. Reuters: Brent settled $34.36 WTI $31.13 on Mar 9 after 24-25% collapse. Mar 16 Brent tumbled 10%+
secondary_factors: COVID demand destruction. Credit and balance-sheet fears for E&P names
store_description: For ConocoPhillips this is one of the clearest cases: the primary driver was the oil shock not just general market weakness. After Brent crashed to $34.36 and WTI to $31.13 on March 9 energy equities remained under intense pressure and March 16's renewed selloff hit COP as investors priced in a severe earnings and cash-flow squeeze.

primary_cause: Semiconductor sector selloff plus growing concern Intel results would be hit by COVID. Published Mar 13 coronavirus update on employee safety. Mar 24 Reuters reported Intel suspended buybacks and warned coronavirus would likely hurt results
secondary_factors: Supply-chain worries. General market panic. Data-center and PC demand uncertainty
store_description: Intel did not preannounce bad numbers in the three days before the drop but the market was clearly moving toward the view that COVID would hit manufacturing and end demand across the chip industry. The later March 24 Reuters report confirming Intel expected a likely hit supports that March 16's 18% decline was anticipatory.

primary_cause: Macro and industrial recession fears. Honeywell reaffirmed Q1 and full-year forecasts Mar 10. Seeing surge in demand for protective face masks. Aerospace and industrial exposure overwhelming positive mask-demand angle
secondary_factors: Broad cyclical industrial selloff. Supply-chain risk. Mar 10 reaffirmation quickly lost credibility as economic shutdown worsened
store_description: Honeywell actually entered the period trying to reassure investors reaffirming outlook on March 10 but that reassurance quickly lost credibility as the economic shutdown worsened. By March 16 the market was likely focused far more on Honeywell's industrial and aerospace cyclicality than on incremental mask demand.

primary_cause: No strong HD-specific negative Mar 13-15. Consumer discretionary and physical retail shutdown fear. Near-20% drop
secondary_factors: Concern about store traffic project deferrals contractor demand. Broad market liquidation. Investors assumed store traffic and big-ticket home-improvement demand could fall sharply
store_description: Home Depot's near-20% drop looks much more like a violent repricing of brick-and-mortar and housing-linked consumer spending than a reaction to one company headline. As March 16 made clear that widespread social restrictions were imminent investors assumed store traffic and big-ticket demand could fall sharply.
